bib.title: A Survey of Resource-efficient LLM and Multimodal Foundation Models

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "A Survey of Resource-Efficient LLM and Multimodal Foundation Models", Mengwei Xu, Wangsong Yin, Dongqi Cai, Rongjie Yi, Daliang Xu, Qipeng Wang, Bingyang Wu, Yihao Zhao, Chen Yang, Shihe Wang, Qiyang Zhang, Zhenyan Lu, Li Zhang, Shangguang Wang, Yuanchun Li, Yunxin Liu, Xin Jin, Xuanzhe Liu (BUPT, PKU, THU). arXiv:2401.08092v2 [cs.LG], 23 Sep 2024 (v1 Jan 2024). Preprint; no venue printed. Related material: github.com/UbiquitousLearning/Efficient_Foundation_Model_Survey.

COVERAGE: 226,000 of 295,386 chars read line by line, covering all of the body from the abstract to the conclusions (body ends about char 41,000 of the reference-free text, i.e. ~38 pages). The remaining ~69k chars are the reference list (refs [205]-[497]). I read only the tail of it (last 1,500 chars) and a short slice. There is no appendix. The extraction is clean text, not garbled. Page numbers below are the printed page.

TAXONOMY (the survey's Fig. 2, p.3)
- Section 2: foundation model overview (language, vision, multimodal) with cost analysis.
- Section 3, architectures: efficient attention (sparse, approximate, attention-free: SSM/Mamba/RWKV/RetNet); dynamic networks (MoE, early exit); diffusion-specific; ViT-specific.
- Section 4, algorithms:
  - 4.1 pre-training: data reduction, NAS, progressive learning, mixed precision.
  - 4.2 fine-tuning: additive (adapter/prompt/prefix), selective, re-parameter (LoRA family).
  - 4.3 inference: opportunistic decoding (speculative, look-up), input filtering/compression (prompt compression, token pruning), KV cache, long context.
  - 4.4 compression: pruning (structured, unstructured, contextual), distillation (black-box, white-box), quantization (QAT, PTQ weight-only, PTQ weight+activation), low-rank decomposition.
- Section 5, systems: distributed training; federated learning; serving on cloud (5.3: inference accelerating, memory saving, emerging platforms); serving on edge (5.4).
- Section 6: open directions (cloud-edge hybrid, activation sparsity, LLM-as-a-service, agents as a system to optimize, privacy, scaling law).

CLAIMS (ranked for inference serving; nearly all numbers are results the survey cites from other papers, not its own measurements)

- claim: KV cache memory formula, in single precision.
  number: B x S x D x L x 2 x 4 bytes
  setup: B batch, S sequence length, D hidden dim, L decoder layers; 2 = K and V; 4 = FP32 bytes (use 2 for FP16).
  quote: "the memory required for storing the KV cache in single-precision format can be calculated as (B × S × D × L × 2 × 4) Bytes"
  where: p.7 (about char 17,500)

- claim: Attention FLOPs are quadratic and FFN FLOPs linear in sequence length; the GPT-2 profile shows FFN above attention at short length and the gap closing at long length.
  number: attention O(T²D), FFN O(TD²); at T=1024, attention 99,164 vs FFN 118,702 (Fig. 5 table, units as printed, not stated).
  setup: GPT-2, flops-profiler tool.
  quote: "the computation complexity of attention is O(T 2D), while that of FFN is O(T D2), where T represents the sequence length and D the hidden state dimension"
  where: p.7

- claim: Quantization speed and throughput numbers cited for serving.
  number: ATOM 7.73x vs FP16, 2.53x vs INT8; llama.cpp K-quant 3-4x vs FP16
  setup: ATOM = 4-bit weight-activation quantization, end-to-end serving throughput at the same latency target. K-quant on llama.cpp, likely CPU/edge. Hardware and model not given in the survey.
  quote: "ATOM on 4-bit weight-activation quantization improves end-to-end throughput by up to 7.73 × compared to the FP16 and by 2.53× compared to INT8 quantization, while maintaining the same latency target." / "performing model inference using K-quant quantization is approximately 3-4 × faster than inference with the original FP16 model."
  where: p.29-30 (about chars 140,000-142,000)

- claim: Accuracy cost of 4-bit weight+activation quantization is not free.
  number: 8.4% accuracy loss (LLM-FP4, LLaMA-13B); GPTQ 3-4 bits on 175B "minimal accuracy loss"
  setup: LLM-FP4 quantizes weights and activations to 4-bit floating point. GPTQ is weight-only.
  quote: "LLM-FP4 successfully quantizes both weights and activations in the LLaMA-13B to only 4-bit and achieves only 8.4% accuracy loss than the full-precision model."
  where: p.30-31

- claim: Quantization formula (absmax scaling) and the point that engines often skip dequantization by using integer matmul.
  number: none
  setup: Eq. (2)-(3); ggml/Intel use CPU SIMD integer matmul; bitsandbytes/QNN for GPU/NPU.
  quote: "DNN engines frequently exploit the integer computation capabilities of accelerators to directly execute matrix multiplication on quantized weights and activations, thereby accelerating computations."
  where: p.29

- claim: Speculative decoding is lossless and gives 2-3x; variants report 1.7-2.1x.
  number: 2-3x (Leviathan, T5X); 70B Chinchilla similar (Chen); SpecTr 2.13x wall clock; Draft & Verify 1.73x (Llama-2); LLMA over 2x
  setup: a small draft model proposes γ tokens, the large model verifies them in parallel. Medusa, Lookahead and Draft & Verify need no separate draft model.
  quote: "this process ensures complete accuracy, and the final decoding results are identical to those achieved using only Mp. Yaniv et al. [209] achieves 2-3× improvement using speculative decoding on the T5X model."
  where: p.23

- claim: KV cache compression and eviction results.
  number: H2O latency up to 1.9x and throughput 29x; Scissorhands KV memory up to 5x reduction; Dynamic Context Pruning up to 2x throughput; vAttention up to 1.29x throughput over vLLM
  setup: H2O is attention-score-based eviction vs "robust baselines" (not named). Scissorhands "while maintaining model quality." vAttention relies on OS/CUDA paging instead of a custom kernel.
  quote: "H2O demonstrates the capability to reduce latency by up to 1.9× and increase throughput by 29×." / "achieving up to a 5× reduction while maintaining model quality" / "improves the end-to-end serving throughput by up to 1.29 × compared to vLLM"
  where: p.25

- claim: Sparse attention does not by itself shrink KV memory.
  number: none
  setup: conceptual point.
  quote: "most sparse attention designs, which primarily target the reduction of computational complexity [36, 464], do not necessarily lead to a reduction in KV cache memory consumption."
  where: p.25

- claim: Cloud serving taxonomy (5.3) maps to concrete systems.
  number: none
  setup: Kernels (FlashAttention for prefill; Flash-Decoding and FlashDecoding++ for decode). Batching (Orca iteration-level scheduling and selective batching; Punica grouped GEMM for multi-LoRA; FastServe preemptive scheduling with KV swap). Prefill/decode (SARATHI and DeepSpeed-FastGen chunked prefill; Splitwise disaggregates prefill and decode). Memory (vLLM PagedAttention; S-LoRA unified paging; SGLang RadixAttention; FlexGen and DeepSpeed-Inference offload to DRAM/NVMe). Platforms (SpotServe on spot instances; HexGen on heterogeneous GPUs).
  quote: "vLLM [199] adopts a block-level on-demand memory allocation mechanism, which only allocates memory to inter-mediate states when needed." / "Splitwise [308] splits the prefill phase and the decoding phase onto different machines according to their different computation and memory requirements."
  where: p.35-36

- claim: Prefix and prompt cache reuse, and prompt compression.
  number: Prompt Cache 8x (GPU) to 60x (CPU); LLMLingua up to 20x compression; Mooncake, CacheGen and CachedAttention are listed with no numbers
  setup: Prompt Cache precomputes attention states for frequent segments. Gains are latency, with output unchanged.
  quote: "The enhancements vary from an 8× improvement for GPU-based inference to a 60× improvement for CPU-based inference, all while preserving output accuracy" / "LLMLingua can achieve up to 20 × compression with minimal performance loss."
  where: p.24

- claim: Training-cost context numbers.
  number: LLaMA-2-70B 1.7 million GPU hours, 2.5x10^12 J, 291 t CO2e; NVIDIA 1.5M AI servers/yr by 2027 at 85.4 TWh/yr
  setup: pre-training; the energy projection is from de Vries (Joule 2023).
  quote: "the pre-training of LLaMa-2-70B takes 1.7× millions of GPU hours and consumes 2.5 × 1012 Joules of energy." / "would consume at least 85.4 terawatt-hours of electricity annuall"
  where: p.2
  Caution: the survey elsewhere says "0.3 trillion tokens for GPT-3-175B" (p.18, section 4.1.1), which looks like a slip. I did not verify it.

- claim: Edge and on-device memory is the bottleneck.
  number: 8 GB device memory example; PowerInfer up to 11x over llama.cpp (a 40B model at ten tokens per second on a PC)
  setup: PowerInfer splits hot neurons (GPU) from cold neurons (CPU) using activation sparsity.
  quote: "PowerInfer achieves up to 11× acceleration, enabling the 40B model to output ten tokens per second on a personal computer."
  where: p.27

- claim: Architecture alternatives to attention.
  number: Mamba 5x speed; RetNet 25-50% training memory saving and 7x acceleration
  setup: as claimed by the cited papers; the survey does not say what the Mamba baseline or hardware was.
  quote: "This model achieves a notable 5 × speed increase over traditional transformers and exhibits linear scaling with sequence length."
  where: p.15

- claim: Cost breakdown of multimodal modules.
  number: Vicuna-7B 7B params, 14 GB, 312 GFLOPs per sample; image encoder 0.63B params, 2.4 GB, 167.59 GFLOPs; Stable Diffusion 2.1 U-Net 865M params, 759 GFLOPs per sample
  setup: Fig. 6 and 7, ImageBind and PandaGPT modules, 10-token prompt for SD.
  quote: "this model consists of 7B parameters, occupies 14G memory, and with total GFLOPs of 312 for processing a sample"
  where: p.12-13

LIMITS
- It is a survey: it ran no new serving benchmarks. Almost every speedup is the cited paper's own claim. Hardware, baselines and batch size are mostly missing, and gains from different papers cannot be compared.
- The scope is stated as algorithm and system work only, with hardware design excluded. It covers physical resources only, mainly papers from CSRankings top venues plus hand-picked arXiv papers, mostly from 2020 onward.
- Material cutoff is about 2023 to mid-2024 (a few 2024 items: QuaRot, EfficientQAT, I-LLM, SpinQuant, DeepSeek-V2, Mooncake). It has dated since: no FP8 or MXFP4 serving, no EAGLE-style speculative decoding, and no RL or reasoning-model serving. Section 4.3.1 uses Medusa and lookahead only. Treat its "state of the art" as early 2024.
- The speculative-decoding description has a notation slip: it says "decode γ tokens by Mp", although the draft model Mq should do the drafting.
- The edge section is thin and has no numbers. The cloud serving section (5.3) is about 1.5 pages and qualitative, with no tables.
- Unverified details: pruning/quantization per-model accuracy, and a slip in the PowerInfer/SIGE reference ("SIGE [352]" duplicates the UPop citation id).

BUILDS ON (as printed)
- Quantization and compression: Dettmers et al. 2022 LLM.int8(); GPTQ (Frantar et al. 2022); AWQ [243]; SmoothQuant [424]; QLoRA (Dettmers et al. 2023).
- Serving: Orca [458]; vLLM / PagedAttention (Kwon et al. 2023); FlashAttention (Dao et al. 2022) and FlashAttention-2 (Dao 2023); Flash-Decoding (Dao et al. 2023); FlexGen [351]; DeepSpeed-Inference [21].
- Speculative decoding: Leviathan et al. [209]; Chen et al. 2023.
- Prior surveys named as overlapping: Kim et al. 2023 "Full stack optimization of transformer inference: a survey"; Ding et al. 2023 "The efficiency spectrum of large language models"; Fournier et al. "A practical survey on faster and lighter transformers" (ACM Computing Surveys, 2023); Koilia and Kachris 2024 (hardware acceleration of LLMs).
- Scaling law: Kaplan et al. 2020.

CODE: None. Equations only. Eq. (2) quantize: X_IntN = Round(2^N / absmax(X_FP32) x X_FP32) = Round(c_FP32 x X_FP32); Eq. (3) dequantize: X_FP32 = X_IntN / c_FP32 (p.29). Table 5 (p.33) lists open-source frameworks and what each supports. Notable entries: TensorRT-LLM (AWQ, GPTQ, SmoothQuant, speculative decoding, PagedAttention), HF TGI, vLLM, LightLLM, LMDeploy, llama.cpp (2-8 bit integer quantization), MLC-LLM.

FIGURES (all PNG-based; I did not run the captions script, so these are taken from the extracted caption text)
- Fig. 2, p.3: survey organization tree. Fastest way to see the full taxonomy.
- Fig. 4, p.7: weight and FLOPs proportion by component (embedding/LM head, attention, FFN, conv) for BERT, GPT-2, T5, wav2vec2, Llama-7B at sequence length 128. Embedding is ~25% of storage, with minimal compute.
- Fig. 5, p.7: GPT-2 inference FLOPs against token length (attention vs FFN).
- Fig. 12, p.19: full method tree for algorithms. Best single-page index of KV, quantization and decoding papers.
- Fig. 15, p.26: compression techniques diagram (PTQ vs QAT, structured and unstructured pruning, white-box and black-box KD).
- Fig. 16, p.32: systems taxonomy (serving on cloud/edge).
- Table 4, p.14: time and space complexity of Transformer, Reformer, Hyena, SSM, RetNet, RWKV.
- Table 5, p.33: open-source frameworks, each marked cloud, edge, training or inference.

PROBLEMS: None serious. No embedded instructions found in the text. Figure content (charts for Fig. 4, 6 and 7) is not in the text extraction, so only their descriptions and the caption text were read; the values behind the bars are not available.
